Frequently Asked Questions
How should I interpret Turnitin's AI writing percentage and false positives?
The percentage shown in the AI writing report is the amount of qualifying text within the submission that Turnitin’s AI writing 
detection model determines was either likely AI-generated text from a large-language model or likely AI-generated text that was 
likely revised using an AI paraphrase tool or word spinner.
 
False positives (incorrectly flagging human-written text as AI-generated) are a possibility in AI models.
 
AI detection scores under 20%, which we do not surface in new reports, have a higher likelihood of false positives. To reduce the 
likelihood of misinterpretation, no score or highlights are attributed and are indicated with an asterisk in the report (*%).

What does 'qualifying text' mean?
Our model only processes qualifying text in the form of long-form writing. Long-form writing means individual sentences contained in paragraphs that make up a

highlighted in cyan in the submission, and likely AI-generated and then likely AI-paraphrased will be highlighted purple.
 
Non-qualifying text, such as bullet points, annotated bibliographies, etc., will not be processed and can create disparity between the submission highlights and the 
percentage shown.

Next-Generation EMR System: Blockchain and 
Multimedia Communication Technologies 
  Raman Nag N                            
Computer Science and Engineering 
Siddaganga Institute of Technology 
Tumakuru, Karnataka, India 
raman.nag.n2005@gmail.com 
 
 
 
Shruthi K  
Computer Science and Engineering 
Siddaganga Institute of Technology 
Tumakuru, Karnataka, India 
shruthik@sit.ac.in 
Abstract— Hospital-centric data management has long 
created a situation where patients remain dependent on 
individual institutions for access to their own clinical 
histories. Record portability between hospitals is limited; 
server outages or cyberattacks can result in irreversible 
data loss; and multimedia clinical files such as imaging 
scans and consultation recordings fall outside what 
conventional 
text-based 
EMR 
architectures 
can 
accommodate. This paper describes the design and 
evaluation of a decentralized Electronic Medical Record 
platform constructed on Ethereum-compatible smart 
contracts together with IPFS-based off-chain storage. The 
system separates content storage from access governance 
— actual medical files are kept on IPFS through Pinata, 
whereas only their content identifiers are anchored on-
chain. Six Solidity contracts partition responsibility 
across doctor management, patient records, hospital 
registration, insurance processing, research consent, and 
system 
administration. 
Patients 
authenticate 
via 
MetaMask wallets and determine, at the granularity of 
individual transactions, which clinicians may retrieve 
which records. Access requests from insurance entities 
and research bodies are processed only upon explicit 
patient authorization. Prototype evaluation spanning 
seven file formats — MP4, DICOM, JPEG, PNG, WAV, 
M4A, and PDF — recorded an average retrieval rate of 
0.93 MB/s, an upload rate of 0.72 MB/s across 314 KB of 
test data, and a cumulative efficiency ratio of 92.54. The 
results indicate that off-chain multimedia storage paired 
with on-chain access governance can satisfy both 
functional 
security 
requirements 
and 
practical 
throughput constraints in healthcare settings. 
Keywords – IPFS, EMR, Decentralization multimedia, Blockchain  
 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Healthcare Digital health infrastructure has grown rapidly 
across hospitals and clinics, yet the underlying storage model 
for patient records has barely changed data still lives on 
servers owned by individual institutions, cut off from other 
hospitals and fully opaque to the patient. Electronic Medical 
Records (EMR) act as structured digital repositories of a 
patient's clinical journey, holding diagnoses, laboratory 
results, prescribed medications, and medical imaging. The 
problem is not the concept of an EMR but its implementation: 
nearly every deployment is centralized within a single 
hospital's control as shown in fig 1, which creates 
fragmentation 
of 
records 
across 
institutions, 
poor 
interoperability, and exposure to localized failures or attacks 
[1]. Multimedia data adds a further dimension to this 
challenge. MRI sequences, surgical recordings, and 
diagnostic audio cannot be efficiently stored or retrieved 
through text-oriented database systems, yet their clinical 
importance continues to rise. 
 
Figure. 1. Traditional vs Proposed Blockchain-Based 
EHR System 
Smart contracts offer a technically concrete path through 
these problems. Deployed on a blockchain network, they are 
programs whose execution logic is fixed at deployment and 
no administrator can silently modify access rules after the 
fact. Every transaction is cryptographically signed and forms 
part of a permanent, auditable chain. Multiple hospitals can 
read from and write to the same distributed ledger under 
defined permission constraints, which provides a shared trust 
infrastructure that centralized databases cannot replicate. 
Blockchain's relevance in this domain stems precisely from 
the gap that conventional databases leave: patient-controlled, 
cross-institutional, tamper-evident access to medical records. 
This paper proposes a blockchain-based multimedia EMR 
architecture that combines Ethereum smart contract access 
governance with decentralized file storage through the 
InterPlanetary File System. Five stakeholder categories such 
as patients, doctors, hospitals, insurance providers, and 
research institutions all interact through role-specific 
interfaces. Large multimedia files are stored on IPFS while 
their cryptographic hash references are recorded on-chain, 
preserving data integrity without inflating blockchain 
storage costs. 
A. Organization of Paper 
The Section II surveys related work. Section III presents the 
proposed system architecture and implementation detail. 
Section IV reports experimental results and performance

II. RELATED WORK 
Recent advancements in blockchain technology and 
multimedia communication have significantly influenced 
secure healthcare data management systems. Several 
researchers have proposed different models focusing on data 
privacy, decentralized storage, and cross-institutional 
medical data sharing. However, many challenges such as 
patient-controlled consent, multimedia scalability, and multi-
stakeholder workflows still remain open.  
Mahajan and Junnarkar [2] integrated lightweight elliptic 
curve cryptography with a private blockchain to protect 
biomedical images across edge, fog, and cloud computing 
tiers. Encryption efficiency is demonstrably strong. The 
critical gap is that patient authorization is entirely absent: 
permission management resides with institutions rather than 
with patients, which reproduces the centralized trust model in 
a distributed guise. No mechanism exists for patients to grant 
or withdraw access independently.  
Wu, Dwivedi, and Srivastava [3] proposed a theoretical 
framework coupling the POPPAC access control model with 
blockchain to protect private medical information. The 
conceptual design is well-argued. Its limitation is practical: 
no prototype was built, insurance and research organization 
workflows are unaddressed, and cloud storage is assumed 
throughout — a choice that sacrifices decentralization at the 
storage layer even while blockchain handles the access layer. 
Zhao et al. [4] introduced StuChain, a student e-portfolio 
platform using a hybrid RBAC-ABAC access model, with 
demonstrated scalability. The architecture cannot transfer 
cleanly to healthcare. Patient consent management, clinical 
multimedia storage, and insurance claim processing are 
structurally absent from StuChain's design, not incidentally 
omitted. Adapting it would require near-complete redesign of 
its core permission model. 
Mole and Shaji [5] deployed an Ethereum and IPFS-based 
EHR system and reported favorable throughput and latency 
figures. A significant architectural concern, however, is that 
patient records are maintained on a local Ganache 
development server — a tool designed for testing, not 
production. This choice reintroduces centralized data custody 
through the backend, while multimedia clinical files and 
research workflows fall entirely outside the system's scope. 
Shuaib et al. [6] built a permissioned blockchain EHR sharing 
system using IBFT consensus and threshold signatures, 
achieving measurable improvements over proof-of-work 
alternatives. Despite this, permission control rests with 
miners and care providers rather than patients. A patient 
cannot independently revoke access; institutional mediation 
remains necessary, and insurance-related workflows are 
entirely absent from the implementation. 
Landolsi, Hlaoua, and Ben Romdhane [7] produced a 
thorough survey of NLP-based information extraction from 
clinical documents, covering rule-based, statistical, and 
transformer-based approaches including BioBERT. The 
extracted information itself carries no protection in this 
survey context — there is no access control mechanism and 
no tamper-proofing, so the extracted output could be retrieved 
or altered by unauthorized parties. 
Chelladurai, Pandian, and Ramasamy [8] designed a patient-
centric EHR system using blockchain-stored metadata hashes 
and tamper-evident access logs. Integrity verification is 
addressed well. The system does not extend to research 
consent management, insurance processing, or decentralized 
multimedia storage — coverage that any production-ready 
clinical platform would require. 
Puneeth and Parthasarathy [9] reviewed more than 150 
blockchain-based EHR papers, identifying interoperability, 
scalability, and access control as persistent open challenges. 
The value of this contribution is its systematic mapping of the 
field. Its limitation is that it proposes no engineering solution 
to any of the problems it documents. 
Looking across these works, a clear gap emerges existing 
systems Across these works, a recurring structural gap is 
visible. Systems that prioritize security often do so at the cost 
of patient agency. Systems that emphasize decentralized 
storage rarely address the full set of stakeholders involved in 
clinical data flows. Patient-controlled consent, verified 
multimedia storage, and coordinated support for hospitals, 
insurers, and researchers have not been integrated into a 
single deployable architecture. The present work addresses 
that gap directly, through six coordinated smart contracts 
operating over IPFS-based distributed storage. 
III. PROPOSED SYSTEM 
 
A. Existing System  
 
 
 
 
 
Centralized Storage and Limited Security: 
Present EMR deployments rely on institution-
managed 
databases — an 
architecture that 
concentrates risk at single points. Unauthorized 
access, data tampering, and server-level failures are 
not hypothetical edge cases; they represent 
documented recurring incidents across healthcare 
systems 
globally. 
Cross-institutional 
record 
verification is additionally impeded by the absence 
of any shared trust layer, which forces hospitals onto 
incompatible data schemas with no standard 
mechanism for interchange. 
 
 
Multimedia Handling and Access Control Gaps: 
Traditional healthcare systems struggle with 
securely storing multimedia medical files, lack 
patient-controlled access, and offer no structured 
role-based permission management for doctors, 
hospitals, insurers, and researchers — all of which 
the proposed system resolves through blockchain-
based immutable storage, IPFS-based decentralized 
multimedia management, and smart contract-driven 
access control. 
 
B. Scope of the System 
 
 
       
The proposed platform targets four functional 
objectives simultaneously. First, it enables 
cross-institutional 
data 
sharing 
without 
requiring direct trust between hospitals, by 
anchoring access governance in a distributed

server. Second, it places access permission

medical files through IPFS, keeping on-chain

C. Materials and Methods 
 
The architecture integrates three coordinated layers: a React-
based frontend, an Ethereum smart contract network, and 
IPFS-based distributed file storage, with MetaMask handling 
transaction signing throughout. The structural decision to 
decouple file storage from access metadata was foundational. 
Storing binary medical files on-chain is both technically 
impractical, file sizes exceed reasonable block data limits and 
economically unsustainable given gas cost structures. IPFS 
resolves this by assigning each uploaded file a content 
identifier (CID) derived from a cryptographic hash of the 
file's contents. That CID, rather than the file itself, is written 
to the blockchain, providing an unforgeable reference that 
simultaneously functions as an integrity checksum. 
The system block diagram as shown in fig 2 spans five layers. 
The User Layer encompasses all role-based stakeholder 
interaction. The Application Layer runs the React single-page 
interface with separate dashboard views for each role. The 
Blockchain Layer hosts the six Solidity contracts on 
Ethereum. The Multimedia Storage Layer is managed 
through IPFS via Pinata's pinning service. The Verification 
Layer operates at retrieval time, re-hashing downloaded files 
and comparing results against the stored CIDs to detect any 
modification. 
 
Figure 2. System Architecture of the Multimedia EHR System 
Frontend Layer: The React interface provides distinct role-
specific dashboards rather than a single filtered view. This 
separation is not cosmetic, conflating views at the interface 
layer risks blurring the permission boundaries enforced at the 
contract layer. Doctors access record creation interfaces; 
patients 
view 
and 
control 
their 
permission 
logs; 
administrators manage registration and approval queues. The 
frontend listens to smart contract events, updating dashboard 
state in real time without manual refresh. 
Wallet and Transaction Layer: Authentication is handled 
entirely through MetaMask, eliminating any server-side 
session state or password database. Each stakeholder action 
generates a blockchain transaction signed by the user's private 
key before submission. This makes every recorded action 
cryptographically attributable and removes the login server as 
a compromise surface. The absence of a centralized credential 
store is itself a security property. 
Blockchain and Smart Contract Layer: The Ethereum 
network provides transaction immutability and deterministic 
contract execution. Smart contracts manage role registration, 
record metadata, and access permissions. Transactions, once 
confirmed, cannot be edited and a property that makes the 
audit trail tamper-proof by construction rather than by policy. 
Contract-emitted events propagate to the frontend, enabling 
live dashboard updates without polling. 
Distributed Storage Layer: Multimedia files are uploaded 
to IPFS through Pinata. Pinata's pinning service ensures that 
content remains persistently available and without active 
pinning, IPFS nodes have no obligation to retain files that no 
node is actively serving. Upon upload, IPFS returns the file's 
CID, which is then stored on-chain. Retrieval reverses this: 
the authorized user requests the CID from the contract, 
fetches the file from IPFS, and the system re-hashes the result. 
Any file modification produces a different hash, failing 
comparison against the on-chain record and flagging the 
retrieval as compromised.

Figure 3. Flow Chart of the Multimedia EHR System 
 
Workflow Description 
Users log in through the React-based interface using their 
MetaMask wallet, where each stakeholder sees a dashboard 
based on their role. Doctors can create records, patients can 
manage access permissions, and administrators can approve 
registrations. When multimedia files such as scans, videos, or 
audio are uploaded, they are stored in IPFS through Pinata, 
which generates a unique CID for each file. This CID, along 
with the record details, is then sent as a transaction to the 
smart contract. Before submission, MetaMask asks the user 
to review and sign the transaction. The smart contract verifies 
the user’s role and permissions, then securely stores the 
record metadata and CID on the blockchain. After 
confirmation, the dashboard updates automatically, and 
authorized users can retrieve files from IPFS using the stored 
CID, while integrity is ensured through hash verification. 
This process maintains a secure and tamper-proof audit trail 
for all medical records. 
 
Algorithm 1:  
 
Figure 4. SHA Algorithm 
Each file entering the system is passed through SHA-256 
before IPFS storage, producing the deterministic hash that 
becomes the CID input. The algorithm processes files as 
follows: the input bit stream is padded to a length congruent 
to 448 bits modulo 512, with a trailing 1 bit, zero bits, and the 
original 64-bit message length appended. This padded 
message is divided into 512-bit blocks. Eight 32-bit state 
variables (H0 through H7) are initialized to constants derived 
from the first eight prime numbers. Each block undergoes 
sixty-four rounds of compression using bitwise rotation, 
XOR, and mixing operations that update the state variables 
continuously. Final concatenation of H0 through H7 produces 
the 256-bit hash output, which the IPFS CID encoder 
transforms into the content identifier anchored on-chain [10]. 
Any modification to the original file produces a detectably 
different hash. 
 
D. Dataset used  
The evaluation dataset was assembled from multiple open 
healthcare repositories to represent the practical range of 
multimedia record types encountered in clinical settings. 
DICOM, JPEG, and PNG imaging files were obtained from 
Zenodo's medical imaging collections and standard radiology 
repositories. 
PDF 
clinical 
documents, 
prescriptions, 
diagnostic reports, and discharge summaries were sourced 
from the PhysioNet MIMIC-III clinical database, which is 
widely used in biomedical informatics research. MP4 video 
files documenting surgical and diagnostic procedures were 
drawn from medical video datasets hosted on Hugging Face. 
WAV audio recordings simulating patient consultation 
exchanges came from publicly accessible healthcare 
communication datasets. The assembled set represents the 
categories a real hospital EMR must handle radiology, 
documentation, procedural video, and patient interaction 
audio sourced from repositories available to academic 
researchers.

In the proposed system, when a clinician uploads a medical 
file, it is stored on IPFS through Pinata, which generates a 
unique CID for that exact file. This CID is then recorded on 
the blockchain along with details such as the uploader and 
timestamp. When an authorized user wants to access the file, 
the system retrieves it from IPFS using the stored CID and 
verifies its integrity through hash matching. If the file has 
been changed in any way, the verification fails. This ensures 
that medical records remain original, secure, and tamper-
proof during transfer without relying on any central 
authority[11]. 
F. Design and implementation of smart contracts 
The proposed system uses six separate Solidity smart 
contracts on Ethereum, with each contract handling a specific 
function. This modular design improves security and makes 
the system easier to manage and update. The EMRSystem 
contract acts as the central coordinator by connecting the 
other 
contracts 
and 
managing 
admin 
roles. 
DoctorManagement handles doctor registration and allows 
approved doctors to create or update patient records. 
PatientManagement stores patient details and lets patients 
control who can access their records. HospitalManagement 
verifies hospitals and links doctors to their institutions. 
InsuranceManagement manages insurance claim requests, 
while ResearchOrganizationManagement handles patient 
consent for research data access. Core operations such as 
record creation, access requests, insurance requests, and 
approval workflows are carried out through these contracts, 
ensuring that the frontend stays updated with the latest system 
activity. 
IV. 
RESULTS AND DISSCUSSION 
 
A. System and Software Requirements 
The development and testing environment required a machine 
with a multi-core processor at 2.0 GHz or above, 8–16 GB 
RAM, and at least 20 GB of available storage to run the full 
stack concurrently web application, local Ethereum node, and 
IPFS services. Frontend development used React with 
Node.js as the runtime. Smart contracts were written in 
Solidity and tested locally against a Ganache node through 
the Hardhat development framework. IPFS integration was 
managed through the Pinata API. Transition from local 
Ganache testing to an Ethereum testnet validated the system's 
behaviour under realistic network conditions.

V. 
CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE 
This work addressed a key gap in existing EMR systems 
by developing and testing a decentralized platform that 
combines patient-controlled access with multimedia 
medical record storage. The system connects patients, 
doctors, hospitals, insurers, and research organizations 
through role-based interfaces, while permission control 
is enforced through smart contracts instead of a 
centralized authority. Record creation, access approval, 
and transaction validation are performed on-chain, 
making the stored data tamper-resistant. Clinical files 
are stored on IPFS, while only their content identifiers 
are recorded on the blockchain to reduce storage cost 
and preserve integrity. Prototype evaluation across 
seven multimedia file formats confirmed the practical 
usability of the system. The platform achieved an 
average retrieval rate of 0.93 MB/s, an overall 
efficiency ratio of 92.54, and contract execution times 
of less than 0.5 seconds across all record types. Even for 
video records, the on-chain overhead remained below 
10%, validating the effectiveness of the off-chain 
storage design. Future work will focus on integration 
with hospital systems, HL7 FHIR interoperability, 
stronger file-level encryption, mobile accessibility, and 
improved scalability. The architecture can also be 
extended to support automated insurance verification 
and secure, consent-based research data sharing.
